slides.title: Before you pay for an AI chatbot, ask *these 5 questions.*
slides.sub: Save this for your next vendor call.

slides.title: Where do its answers come from?
slides.body: It should answer from *your* documents and show which one. If the answer is "the internet", be careful.

slides.title: What happens when it doesn't know?
slides.body: A good assistant says so and hands over to a person. A bad one makes something up, confidently.

slides.title: Where does our data go?
slides.body: Ask where conversations are stored, who can read them, and whether they're used to train anyone's model. Get it in writing.

slides.title: How will we know it's working?
slides.body: Agree the measure up front: questions answered without a human, enquiries captured, time saved. Not "engagement".

slides.title: Who keeps it up to date?
slides.body: Prices, policies and staff change. Ask how the content gets updated, how often, and by whom.

slides.title: The problem

slides.body: Most tool limits are about *where* the work happens. Move the heavy step to something built for it, and keep each tool doing what it's good at.

captions.li:
A small engineering story from our own pipeline this week.

The problem: our automation platform's free plan can't handle files over 5 MB. Our YouTube episodes are 80–90 MB, so scheduled uploads failed and were done by hand.

The fix: split the job in two.
1. The automation platform opens a YouTube resumable upload session (it already holds the authorisation).
2. It passes only the session URL to GitHub.
3. A GitHub Actions job streams the file into that session. No size limit, no extra cost.
4. Videos go up early as private and YouTube publishes them at their slot.

The general lesson: most "tool limits" are about where the work happens. Move the heavy step to something built for it.

If an automation of yours keeps hitting a wall, we're happy to take a look: https://xenovasolutions.com/contact
